newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain Civil Guard official urges crackdown on ETA.
newsitem.headline: Spain Civil Guard official urges crackdown on ETA.

text.p: A senior security official demanded a crackdown on the Basque separatist group ETA on Wednesday after the government ordered heightened security across Spain.
Civil Guard Director General Santiago Lopez Valdivielso said a show of strength, not negotiations, was the appropriate response to a resurgence of attacks blamed on ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).

"The only thing to do about ETA at these times is to deal it as many blows as possible, turn over as many commandos to the judiciary as we can and weaken its infrastructure as much as possible," he said at a police academy in Barcelona.
Spiraling violence which culminated in three killings this week has forced the 29-year-old conflict with ETA back to the top of the government's agenda.

The government has ordered increased police patrols in major cities, more security for judges, politicians and military figures and is seeking help from citizens to combat the violence, official sources told Reuters.

The decision was taken at a meeting of police, Civil Guard and intelligence agents at the Interior Ministry on Tuesday. "The police presence in the streets of some cities will be increased," a government source said.
Madrid, Barcelona, the southern region of Andalusia and the northern Navarra region were among areas targeted for heightened security.
ETA is suspected in five killings so far this year. About 800 people have been killed in the conflict since 1968.
A gunman killrf a Supreme Court judge in Madrid on Monday hours after a car bomb killed a hairdresser going to work at a military base in the southern city of Granada.
A local businessman was shot and killed during carnival celebrations in the Basque town of Tolosa on Tuesday.
A priority for security forces is cracking two ETA cells suspected of recent attacks -- "Comando Madrid" which is active in the Spanish capital and "Comando Donosti" in the Basque country.
Efforts are also concentrated on uncovering two independent cells holding two hostages, official sources said. Police are appealing for help from witnesses.

Despite media reports that Basques are reluctant to serve as jurors in ETA cases, one government source said there was no concern about intimidation of potential witnesses because the information was anonymous.

Though ETA has not claimed responsibilty for any of this week's attacks, some analysts speculated that the resurgence of violence might be motivated by a growing sense of frustration at the nine-month-old government's refusal to negotiate with the group.

The attacks might also be linked to a Supreme Court summons this month of the 25-member leadership of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB) to answer charges of distributing a pro-ETA video in last year's election campaign.

An HB member said last week that Spain would pay the price for the court's action. Two more HB leaders were arrested on Wednesday for failing to appear in court, bringing the number detained to eight.
